qs.q: A patient with Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) presents with a serum sodium of 118 mmol/L, a urine osmolality of 520 mOsm/kg, and is clinically euvolemic. Which ectopic hormone is most likely responsible for this electrolyte derangement?
o: Secretion of arginine vasopressin by tumor cells
Secretion of ectopic erythropoietin by the tumor
qs.e: Ectopic ADH secretion causes SIADH, characterized by euvolemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine. This is a classic paraneoplastic manifestation of small cell lung cancer.

qs.q: A patient diagnosed with Small Cell Lung Cancer develops progressive muscle weakness that paradoxically improves with repeated physical exertion, alongside anti-VGCC antibodies. What is the underlying diagnosis?
qs.e: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by anti-VGCC antibodies that impair presynaptic acetylcholine release. Strength paradoxically improves with repeated stimulation, which differentiates it from myasthenia gravis.

qs.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer develops euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine. What is the ectopic hormone responsible?
qs.e: Ectopic secretion of ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine. PTHrP causes hypercalcemia of malignancy rather than hyponatremia.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with small cell lung cancer develops acute confusion and generalized seizures. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum sodium level of 118 mEq/L, low serum osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine. What is the fundamental mechanism of this patient's electrolyte disturbance?
o: Renal resistance to circulating vasopressin action
Primary renal tubular defect in sodium resorption
Excess antidiuretic hormone causing water retention
qs.e: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion involves autonomous ADH release leading to dilutional hyponatremia. Renal resistance to vasopressin causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus rather than water retention and concentrated urine.

qs.q: A researcher is analyzing the genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer. Which key driver mutation is most frequently identified in adenocarcinomas arising specifically in non-smokers?
qs.e: EGFR mutations are key driver mutations commonly found in lung adenocarcinomas, particularly in patients who have never smoked. KRAS mutations are also seen in adenocarcinoma but are more strongly linked to smoking history.

qs.q: A patient with non-small cell lung cancer has a tumour with a targetable EGFR mutation. What is the expected clinical course after treatment with an EGFR inhibitor?
o: Remarkable response followed by relapse within months to a year
Immediate resistance with no initial response
qs.e: Unresectable adenocarcinomas with EGFR mutations show remarkable responses to inhibitors, but relapse is typical within months to a year due to new mutations or circumventing mechanisms. They are not permanently cured by this therapy alone.

qs.q: What is the primary reason Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) is rarely amenable to surgical resection?
o: It has a tendency to spread early
qs.e: SCLC is rarely resectable because it tends to spread early, often before diagnosis. It is actually highly sensitive to chemotherapy, not resistant, and is a neuroendocrine tumour.

qs.q: Which of the following is a characteristic histological feature of Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)?
o: Tumor displays glandular or squamous architectural patterns.
Cells have scant cytoplasm and finely granular chromatin.
Cells show abundant cytoplasm with prominent nucleoli.
qs.e: SCLC is characterized by scant cytoplasm, small hyperchromatic nuclei, and fine chromatin. Abundant cytoplasm, glandular/squamous architecture, and mucin are features of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC).

es.q: A 55-year-old non-smoking woman is diagnosed with lung cancer. Based on epidemiological data, identify the most likely histological subtype. Additionally, describe the typical clinical presentation and prognosis of Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC).
es.m: The most likely histological subtype of lung cancer in a non-smoking woman is Adenocarcinoma. Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) is almost always metastatic at presentation. It is treated with chemotherapy, and typically has a poor prognosis with a median survival of approximately 1 year.

es.m: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC) is almost always metastatic at presentation (2 marks). Due to its widespread nature, it is typically treated with chemotherapy (1 mark). The prognosis is poor, with a median survival of approximately 1 year (2 marks).

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Small cell lung cancer is a neuroendocrine tumour that grows rapidly, metastasises early and is strongly linked to smoking. It often presents with paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH, Cushing’s, or Lambert‑Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

sections.p: SCLC is a malignant tumour of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells, usually central, that shows small, round cells with scant cytoplasm and neuroendocrine markers on immunohistochemistry.

t.b: Detects central tumour and nodal disease; a mass >1 cm in the hilar region suggests SCLC
Obtains tissue for histology and immunostaining; confirms neuroendocrine phenotype
Hyponatraemia with low plasma osmolality and concentrated urine indicates SIADH, a common paraneoplastic sign

sections.p: SCLC is staged as limited (confined to one hemithorax) or extensive (beyond one hemithorax or distant metastasis).
The single most important risk factor is tobacco smoke. Other factors include occupational exposures and possibly viral infections.
Patients often have a central cough, haemoptysis, or dyspnoea. Paraneoplastic syndromes may dominate the initial presentation.
b: Cushing’s: moon facies, proximal muscle weakness

sections.p: The work‑up focuses on confirming the tumour, staging, and detecting paraneoplastic effects.

t.b: Assesses metabolic activity and distant spread
Elevated ACTH with normal pituitary imaging suggests ectopic source
Hyponatraemia with concentrated urine indicates SIADH

sections.p: Rapid progression, early metastasis, and paraneoplastic syndromes can be life‑threatening.
b: SIADH can lead to severe hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema

sections.p: SCLC is chemosensitive but rarely curable; treatment is systemic and supportive.
b: Platinum (cisplatin or carboplatin) + etoposide – first‑line chemotherapy
Concurrent thoracic radiotherapy in limited stage
Supportive care: anti‑emetics, growth factors, pain control

sections.p: Regular imaging to detect recurrence and counselling to stop smoking.
b: CT chest every 3–6 months for 2 years

sections.p: Other central lung tumours and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma.
b: Large cell carcinoma – similar appearance but less neuroendocrine markers
Squamous cell carcinoma – usually peripheral and keratinising

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal early in disease.
b: Early CT may miss small hilar nodules
Serum sodium can be normal if SIADH is intermittent

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hyponatraemia with confusion or seizures
New onset muscle weakness or autonomic instability

faq.q: Why is smoking the biggest risk factor?
faq.a: Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens that cause DNA mutations in neuroendocrine cells, leading to malignant transformation.
Only in very early limited disease; most patients have metastatic disease at diagnosis and treatment is palliative.

faq.q: What is the role of surgery?
faq.a: Surgery is rarely used because the tumour is usually metastatic at presentation and responds better to chemotherapy.
